newsitem.title: CANADA: BHP poised to decide on diamond sales plan.
newsitem.headline: BHP poised to decide on diamond sales plan.

text.p: Australia's Broken Hill Proprietary Co Ltd plans to decide in the next six months whether to market diamonds from its mine in Canada's Arctic outside the powerful De Beers cartel, officials said Tuesday.

BHP's BHP Diamonds Inc and joint venture partner Dia Met Minerals Ltd expect to begin commercial production of diamonds -- many gem quality -- from their site at Lac de Gras in the Northwest Territories in late 1998.

BHP previously said it was researching all options including selling outside the Central Selling Organization of De Beers Consolidated Mines Ltd which controls about three quarters of the world trade in rough diamonds.
The Australian company, which is making its first foray into diamond mining with the project, and its Canadian partner previously aimed to decide on a marketing strategy by June.
But a decision is now expected in the last half of the year, in part due to the recent arrival of BHP Diamonds' new general manager, Jim Rothwell, a BHP official said.
"We're giving ourselves somewhat of a broad timeframe and saying the second half of this year," BHP Diamonds spokesman Graham Nicholls said.

Dia Met President James Eccott said the decision was pushed back to give Rothwell time to familiarize himself with the Lac de Gras project before finalizing marketing plans. "We're in no great rush," he said.
BHP, which has a 51 percent stake in the project, has said that it would explore all alternatives including independent sales, selling through the CSO or a combination of the two.

"BHP has spent a great deal of time and effort investigating the options open to us and considering strategies that will result in the greatest benefits for the...project and for Canada," Rothwell said in a recent speech.

"In developing a marketing plan, BHP must also ensure compliance with anti-competition regulations in Canada and elsewhere. Discussions with both the federal and territorial governments are ongoing," he said.
Some analysts saw that comment as evidence that BHP is leaning toward selling outside the CSO.

Many analysts and mining officials believe BHP wants to sell its production independently partly because of concerns about potential regulatory problems in the United States where it has major operations. De Beers has a long history of anti-trust brushes with the U.S. Justice Department and has stayed out of the United States for fear of prosecution.
Selling outside the CSO also holds the lure of potentially higher profits for BHP and Dia Met since they would not have to pay the CSO a commission.
Dia Met has 29 percent of the project while the geologists who discovered the deposit and are also major shares holders of Dia Met own the remaining 20 percent outright.

The CSO has made no secret of its desire to bring the Lac de Gras mine into its fold and its officials have met with BHP. The cartel maintains a huge diamond stockpile and seeks to regulate world supply. It boasts that its efforts have yielded higher prices for producers over the long run.

A move by RTZ Corp-CRA Ltd to withdraw its Argyle mine in Australia from the CSO last year spurred speculation that the CSO's grip on the market may be slipping. Any move by BHP to bypass the cartel would be another blow.
Thanks to production from Lac de Gras and other potential diamond mines in the Far North, Canada is expected to eventually become one of the world's top five diamond producers.
The Lac de Gras mine is projected to produce three million to five million carats a year over 25 years with a high proportion of gems, the most profitable segment of the market.
